title: JESUS SAID TO HATE YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER. DID WE MISUNDERSTAND ONE OF HIS MOST DISTURBING COMMANDS?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID TO HATE YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER. DID WE MISUNDERSTAND ONE OF HIS MOST DISTURBING COMMANDS?

The shocking words of Luke 14:26 were never permission to abandon your family. They were a warning about the cost of following Christ—and what happens when the people you love most become the reason you refuse to obey God.
There is a verse in the Bible that sounds almost impossible to reconcile with the Jesus we know.
The Jesus who welcomed children.
The Jesus who commanded us to love our enemies.
The Jesus who, while bleeding on a cross, made sure His mother would be cared for.
That same Jesus looked at a crowd of people and said something that must have made the air go silent.
“If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.” — Luke 14:26 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not a suggestion.
Not a casual observation.
Jesus said such a person cannot be His disciple.
And somewhere, a wounded son is reading those words, remembering the father who abandoned him.
A daughter is remembering the mother whose words still echo through her insecurities.
A wife is thinking about a husband who mocks her faith.
A young believer is remembering the night their family said, “If you choose that Jesus, don't expect us to support you.”
And the question rises from somewhere deep inside the heart.
Jesus, are You really telling me to hate them?
Because if He is, how can the same Lord command us to honor our father and mother?
How can the One who taught forgiveness demand hatred?
And why would the Savior who came to reconcile us to God speak words that seem capable of tearing families apart?
The answer is more beautiful than many people realize.
But it is also more demanding.
Because when we understand what Jesus actually meant, we discover that this verse is not primarily about how much we dislike someone.
It is about whether there is anyone we love so much that we would choose them over Christ.
And that question reaches into places most of us would rather leave untouched.
Before we go any further, we need to return to the scene.
Luke tells us that great multitudes were traveling with Jesus (Luke 14:25).

Imagine the dust rising beneath hundreds of feet. Families walking together. Curious people whispering about miracles. Others wondering whether this extraordinary Teacher might finally deliver the kingdom they had been waiting for.
Some had seen His power.
Some loved His teaching.
Some were fascinated by His reputation.
But Jesus knew something the crowd did not yet fully understand.
Being impressed by Jesus is not the same as being surrendered to Jesus.
So He turned toward them.
And instead of making discipleship sound easier, He revealed its cost.
He spoke about loving Him above family.
He spoke about carrying a cross.
He spoke about counting the cost before beginning a journey.
He was not trying to gather the largest possible audience through comfortable promises.
He was telling the truth about what following Him would require.
And that brings us to the word that has troubled generations.
Hate.
In the Greek text of Luke 14:26, the word translated “hate” comes from μισέω (miseō). In this verse the form is μισεῖ (misei), meaning “hates.”
The word can genuinely mean to hate or detest. We must not pretend that it never carries that meaning.
But words receive their precise force from their context, and Scripture sometimes uses the language of loving and hating to express a comparison of preference, allegiance, or priority.
Consider an earlier passage.

Genesis 29:30–31 describes Jacob's relationship with Rachel and Leah. Verse 30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. The following verse describes Leah as “hated” in the traditional English rendering.
The Hebrew word is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the root שָׂנֵא (sane'), associated with hatred.
Yet the immediate context reveals a contrast between the wife who was loved more and the wife who was loved less.
This does not mean Leah experienced no genuine rejection. She did. It means the language of hatred in that context communicates the painful reality of being comparatively disfavored.
And Jesus Himself gives us the clearest explanation of His meaning.
In Matthew 10:37, He says:
“He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.” (KJV)
There it is.
The parallel teaching does not command emotional cruelty toward our families.
It identifies the issue as supreme allegiance.
Jesus must be loved above everyone else.
Not because our families have no value.
But because no human relationship can rightfully occupy the place that belongs to God.
The point is not that you must stop loving your mother.
It is that you must not love her approval more than you love Christ.
It is not that you must despise your father.
It is that even your father's expectations cannot become the final authority over your conscience when they conflict with God's Word.
It is not that your spouse or children become unimportant.
It is that even the most precious relationships in your life cannot replace the Lord who gave you life.
And perhaps this is where the verse begins to hurt.
Because some of us have never openly denied Jesus.
We have simply learned to become quiet about Him whenever obedience might cost us someone's affection.
We know what Scripture says.
But we also know what our family will say.
We know what obedience requires.
But we are terrified of disappointing the people whose approval we have spent our lives trying to earn.
So we negotiate.
We delay.
We compromise.
We tell ourselves we are keeping the peace.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin allowing another person's acceptance to determine how faithfully we follow Jesus.
That is the danger Christ was exposing.
Not the existence of family love.
The enthronement of family love above the authority of God.
Think about the young man who becomes convinced that Jesus is Lord, but whose family threatens to reject him if he openly follows Christ.
He loves them.
He remembers their sacrifices.
He knows how much they have given him.
He does not want to cause them pain.
And now he faces a decision he never wanted to make.
Will he obey Jesus even if obedience costs him their approval?
Or will he turn away from Christ to preserve the relationship?
Jesus does not treat that decision as insignificant.
He tells us that following Him may sometimes cost us the very relationships we treasure.
In Matthew 10:34–36, Jesus warns that His coming will bring division even within households.
This does not mean He delights in family conflict.
It means the truth about Him will provoke different responses, and those differences can produce painful opposition.
A household may be divided not because the Christian has stopped loving, but because the Christian will not stop believing.
And there is a profound difference.
You can love someone without surrendering your convictions to them.
You can honor your parents without treating their wishes as greater than God's commands.
You can pray for someone who rejects your faith without rejecting your faith to please them.
You can refuse to retaliate even when obedience to Christ makes you misunderstood.
Faithfulness to Jesus does not require hatred toward people. It requires refusing to make people your god.
But someone might still ask:
If Jesus meant supreme allegiance, why did He choose such severe language?
Why not simply say, “Love Me a little more”?
Because Jesus was not describing a small adjustment in our priorities.
He was describing a complete reordering of our lives.
He knew that when loyalty to Him and loyalty to another person came into direct conflict, the choice could feel as severe as losing everything.
The word shocks us because the decision can shake us.
And Jesus refuses to hide that cost.
Notice that Luke 14:26 does not end with parents, spouses, children, brothers, or sisters.
Jesus adds something that exposes an even deeper struggle.
“Yea, and his own life also.”
His own life.
That means the greatest rival to Christ is not always an angry parent or an unbelieving spouse.
Sometimes it is the person staring back at us in the mirror.
Our comfort.
Our reputation.
Our ambitions.
Our carefully protected image.
Our determination to remain in control.
We may say we would follow Jesus anywhere.
Until He leads us somewhere that threatens the life we planned.
We may say we trust Him completely.
Until obedience requires us to surrender something we desperately want to keep.
We may say He is Lord.
Until His Word confronts a habit, relationship, ambition, or secret sin that we have been unwilling to release.
Then the real question emerges.
Do I love Jesus Himself, or do I love the version of Christianity that allows me to remain in charge?
This is why Jesus immediately speaks about carrying a cross.
Luke 14:27 says:
“And whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple.” (KJV)
To the original hearers, a cross was not a decorative symbol.
It was an instrument of Roman execution.
Jesus was not merely speaking about enduring an inconvenient day or an unpleasant personality.
He was describing a willingness to follow Him through suffering, shame, rejection, and even death.
And He wanted the crowd to understand this before they confused enthusiasm with commitment.
He continued with illustrations about a man calculating the cost of building a tower and a king considering whether he could face an approaching army.
His message was unmistakable.
Do not mistake the beginning of discipleship for a promise of an easy life.
Count the cost.
Know whom you are following.
Understand that Jesus is worthy of more than your admiration.
He is worthy of your allegiance.
But now we must address something that matters enormously, especially to those who have been wounded by religious manipulation.
Jesus' command is not permission to abuse, neglect, or abandon your family.
Anyone using Luke 14:26 to justify cruelty has missed the character of the Christ who spoke it.
Jesus affirmed the commandment to honor father and mother (Matthew 15:4).
He condemned religious excuses that allowed people to neglect their parents (Mark 7:9–13).
And while suffering on the cross, He entrusted His mother to the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27).
Think about that.
The Savior who taught that we must love Him above our mothers still demonstrated tender concern for His own mother in His final hours of suffering.
He did not consider love and responsibility beneath Him.
He fulfilled them.
The apostle Paul likewise taught that believers should care for their households (1 Timothy 5:8), and that husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25).
Biblical discipleship does not erase those responsibilities.
It places them under the lordship of Jesus.
And if you are living in an abusive or dangerous situation, this verse does not require you to remain exposed to harm to prove your devotion.
Seeking safety, setting appropriate boundaries, and obtaining trustworthy help are not violations of Christ's command.
Nor does honoring a parent mean obeying demands that are sinful or submitting to mistreatment.
We must never confuse the call to sacrifice for Christ with someone else's demand that we tolerate their cruelty.
The cross Jesus calls us to carry is not a weapon for controlling other people.
It is a call to follow Him.
And following Him means learning to love with truth, courage, holiness, and wisdom.
Now consider something else.
Perhaps you are reading this with a complicated family history.
You love your parents, but they were not always gentle.
You respect your father, but his approval has felt impossible to earn.
You care about your mother, but some of her words left wounds that followed you into adulthood.
Or perhaps you have spent years carrying guilt because someone taught you that being a good Christian means never saying no.
You have mistaken boundaries for rebellion.
You have confused silence with honor.
You have carried responsibility for emotions that were never yours to control.
And now you encounter Jesus saying that He must come first.
At first, the words sound like another impossible demand.
But look more closely.
Christ is not inviting you to become heartless.
He is calling you to stop making your identity dependent on another person's acceptance.
Your father may never say the words you long to hear.
Your mother may never understand the path of obedience God has placed before you.
Someone you love may misunderstand your faithfulness.
But their response does not determine whether you belong to Jesus.
You do not have to be approved by everyone to be faithful to the One who redeemed you.
And for some people, that truth is the beginning of freedom.
Not freedom from loving their family.
Freedom from being ruled by fear of losing their family's approval.
That distinction changes everything.
Because when Christ becomes first, love does not have to disappear.
It can become more truthful.
More courageous.
Less controlled by fear.
You can stop pretending to agree with something you know is wrong.
You can speak with kindness without compromising conviction.
You can forgive without denying that harm occurred.
You can seek reconciliation without pretending that repentance and trust are unnecessary.
You can pray for a family member who has hurt you while recognizing that restored closeness may require time, safety, and genuine change.
And you can remember that even when others refuse reconciliation, you remain responsible for your own conduct before God—not for controlling their choices.
Romans 12:18 expresses this wisdom beautifully:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” (KJV)
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
There are circumstances in which peace is not entirely within your control.
You can pursue it.
You can refuse bitterness.
You can speak truth with love.
But you cannot force another heart to receive what it has decided to reject.
And this brings us to the most important question in the entire passage.
Why is Jesus worthy of such extraordinary devotion?
Why should anyone place Him above the people they love most?
If Jesus were merely another religious teacher, such a demand would be astonishingly inappropriate.
But the Gospels present Him as far more than a teacher.
He is the Son of God.
The eternal Word who became flesh (John 1:1, 14).
The One through whom all things were made (John 1:3).
The Savior who came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
The One who gave Himself for sinners and rose again.
His claim upon our lives is inseparable from who He is.
He does not demand supreme allegiance as a competing human authority trying to steal our affection.
He calls us to the rightful worship and obedience owed to God.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The Jesus who asks you to surrender everything is the Jesus who first gave Himself to save you.
He did not stand at a safe distance from suffering and demand that His followers endure what He refused to face.
He entered our broken world.
He experienced rejection.
He was misunderstood by people close to Him.
He was betrayed by a friend.
He was abandoned by disciples.
He was falsely accused, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
And He willingly endured the cross to accomplish our redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we perfectly reordered every affection in our hearts.
Christ died for sinners.
That is grace.
And grace does not make discipleship meaningless.
Grace makes discipleship possible.
We do not earn salvation by demonstrating that we love Jesus more than our parents.
We are saved by God's grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us also begins to transform our loyalties, desires, and obedience.
Jesus does not purchase our salvation with His blood and then leave us unchanged.
He calls us to follow Him.
To repent.
To trust Him.
To surrender the throne of our hearts.
And when we fail, we do not have to hide from the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
We return to Him in repentance and faith.
Perhaps you have already failed this test.
Perhaps you remained silent when you knew you should have spoken.
Perhaps you compromised because you were afraid of rejection.
Perhaps you allowed someone else's opinion to become more important than God's Word.
Or perhaps you have made your own desires the final authority over your life.
Listen carefully.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
Remember Peter.
He boldly insisted that he would remain loyal to Jesus.
Then, when the pressure became terrifying, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own voice.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization that the man who had promised faithfulness had collapsed under fear.
Yet Peter's failure was not the end.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored him and called him again to shepherd His people (John 21:15–19).
The same Peter who denied Christ would later proclaim Him publicly.
That is not a story about how strong Peter was.
It is a testimony to the mercy and transforming power of Jesus.
And maybe that is the word someone needs today.
Your worst moment of compromise does not have to become your permanent identity.
You can repent.
You can return.
You can begin obeying where you once surrendered to fear.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than your failure is a master.
From denial to restoration.
From fear to faithfulness.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And yet, we must not turn that beautiful truth into an excuse to remain unchanged.
The same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner also calls that sinner to a new way of life.
So here is the question I want you to sit with.
Not the question you would answer publicly to impress other Christians.
The question you would answer alone, with your Bible open and no one watching.
Who has the power to make you disobey Jesus simply because you are afraid of losing them?
Maybe it is a parent.
Maybe it is a spouse.
Maybe it is a romantic relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is a group of friends whose acceptance has become more important than your convictions.
Maybe it is not another person at all.
Maybe it is your own pride.
Your comfort.
Your fear.
Your secret attachment to a life you do not want to surrender.
Whatever it is, bring it into the light.
Not to impress God with your strength.
But to confess your need for His mercy.
You might pray something as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, You know the people I love and the fears I carry. You know how deeply I want to be accepted. Forgive me for the times I have placed another voice above Yours. Teach me to honor my family without compromising Your truth. Heal what is wounded in my relationships. Give me courage where I am afraid, humility where I am proud, and wisdom where obedience is difficult. I do not want to use Your Word as an excuse for cruelty, and I do not want to use my love for people as an excuse for disobedience. Be first in my heart. Teach me to follow You faithfully. Amen.”
And if this passage has exposed something you have been wrestling with, you do not have to pretend.
You do not need to reveal private details or explain wounds you are not ready to discuss.
Sometimes a few sincere words can open the door for another struggling believer to realize they are not alone.
And if God has helped you love your family faithfully while standing firm in your convictions, your testimony may encourage someone facing that same struggle.
There is one more thing I do not want you to miss.
Jesus never said that loving Him first would guarantee that your family would understand.
He never promised that everyone would applaud your obedience.
He never told us that discipleship would be free from tears.
But He did promise that those who lose relationships or earthly security for His sake are not forgotten by God (Mark 10:29–30).
That promise must be read alongside His warning about persecution, not as a guarantee of wealth or an easy replacement for every loss.
And it points us toward something larger than the approval of this present world.
The kingdom of God.
The family of faith.
The life to come.
The Lord who will never abandon His people.
Perhaps the people closest to you do not understand your love for Jesus.
Perhaps you have been called foolish, extreme, or ungrateful because you refused to compromise a biblical conviction.
Perhaps you have wept over relationships that changed when you began taking your faith seriously.
Christ sees.
And your suffering does not make Him indifferent.
But remember this as well.
Do not turn your faithfulness into pride.
Do not use the truth as an excuse to become harsh.
Do not confuse winning arguments with bearing witness to Christ.
Let your family see patience.
Let them see integrity.
Let them see that following Jesus makes you more truthful, more responsible, more compassionate, and more willing to serve.
Let your obedience be unmistakable.
And let your love remain genuine.
Because the goal is not to prove that you can live without your family.
The goal is to prove, through your life, that Jesus is worthy of first place.
Someone may be using this passage to justify cruelty.
Someone else may be silently struggling to follow Jesus because their family does not approve.
Our desire is not merely to gather readers.
It is to help people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ, understand His Word, and grow in a faith that endures beyond a moment of inspiration.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who are hungry to know Christ more deeply.

Scripture encourages believers to support faithful ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Those products are a small expression of our appreciation.
The greater purpose is the Gospel.
The Scriptures explained faithfully.
The struggling believer encouraged.
The searching soul pointed toward Christ.
The person who thought their story was over discovering that God's grace is still at work.
Because at the end of our lives, the greatest question will not be whether everyone approved of us.
It will be whether we truly belonged to the Christ we claimed to follow.
So return with me to the words that first disturbed us.
“If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother…”
They sound so severe until we understand what Jesus is asking.
He is not commanding you to become less loving.
He is commanding you to recognize who deserves your highest love.
He is not calling you to abandon compassion.
He is calling you to surrender competing allegiances.
He is not asking you to become cruel to the people who raised you.
He is asking whether you will still follow Him when those people cannot understand your obedience.
And He is not asking you to make a sacrifice He knows nothing about.
He is the crucified and risen Savior who gave Himself for you.
So love your father.
Honor your mother.
Cherish your spouse.
Care for your children.
Pray for your family.
Seek peace wherever possible.
Forgive as Christ has forgiven you.
But never place any of them on the throne that belongs to Jesus alone.
Because the greatest gift you can give your family is not a version of yourself that will compromise everything to keep them pleased.
It is a life genuinely transformed by the grace and truth of Christ.
And if you have stumbled along the way, remember Peter.
The Savior who restored a denying disciple is still able to restore those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
The cross is not the end of the story.
The empty tomb declares that Jesus is alive.
And because He lives, surrender is not the death of hope.
It is the beginning of a life that belongs to Him.
You were never commanded to stop loving the people who gave you a place in this world—you were called to love Jesus above everyone, because He alone can give you eternal life.
